name: Aaron Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and this is confidential; your name won't go in our findings. Could you walk me through a normal workday, from when you arrive?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, 43, a junior lineworker for the electric company. We meet at the depot before daylight, check the truck and work order, then drive out to the line; I carry gear, set cones and climb when the crew lead says it's safe.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What parts of it do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing the lights come back on after a storm and knowing the crew did it right. The cold hours are hard, and I still replay a safety check in my head at home. My partner Mara and I have two children, ages 10 and 13, and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds close to what I see now: a new screen on the truck, then the same wet gloves outside. I would tell the crew the work still needs people who know when a line is unsafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the software can sort a work order, but someone still has to stand under the wire and check the ground. The lights coming back on after a storm are still earned by the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think this small version takes my job, because most of my shift is physical and supervised. I'm still short on savings, though, so a slow month or a mortgage payment rise would hurt more than a new app helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep showing up and get better at the safety steps my lead teaches me. I would put a little aside after each pay, but I couldn't promise a fixed amount every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady about the job, but tight in the chest when I add up mortgage and truck fare. It's not AI that has me checking my balance before payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or cost is hardest to cover when the month runs long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage comes first, and then fuel for getting to the depot before the buses run. If a tool breaks at home, we wait until next pay instead of putting it on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When a new screen or process arrives at the depot, how do you handle it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask the crew lead to show me the safe way once, then I do it on paper beside the screen. I'm not keen to trust a machine before I know what it records.

say: I say the **crew** still checks what a screen cannot see beside a live line.
I tell friends a small app change doesn't remove the **field work**.
think: I don't expect this version to take my **job**, because my shift is mostly physical.
I still worry about **the mortgage** because our savings would not cover a full month.
do: Keep learning the crew's **safety steps** on each callout.
Set aside a small amount after **payday** when bills allow.
feel: The work feels steady, while **mortgage and fuel** keep the month tight.
S0.quote: The lights coming back on after a storm are still earned by the crew.
fieldNote: He separates small **screen changes** from the physical task of restoring power.
His calm tone sits beside a thin **cash buffer** and close attention to basic bills.

steps.text: Keep learning the crew's safety checks on storm callouts
Set aside spare pay after the mortgage and fuel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the office using it to plan which crew goes where or check a work order faster. We would still put up barriers and test the line before touching anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster planning is useful if the crew can correct a bad route before anyone climbs. A screen can't take responsibility for a safe work zone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning desk may need fewer people, and that could change who gets assigned to crews. My job is less exposed today, but a junior worker is easy to leave off a roster if work gets tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current job and ask for more supervised pole time, so the lead sees I can handle the basics. I'd ask the union rep how crew assignments are decided if software starts routing calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about hours more than about a robot tomorrow. I don't have enough savings to take a long course or miss several weeks of pay with a mortgage and two children at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What specific change to the work order would make you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A route that says a stretch is clear when the last crew reported a fallen branch. I want a person to call the dispatcher and confirm before we drive out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union rep to find out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether an automated roster can cut junior hours without a person explaining why. I would want a way to appeal a bad assignment, not a promise that nothing will change.

say: I say **faster planning** helps only when a crew can correct a bad route.
I remind friends a person still owns the **safety decision** at the pole.
think: I worry a junior worker may lose **hours** if crews are assigned by software.
I can't take a long course without **income** to cover the mortgage.
do: Ask for more **supervised pole time** with the crew lead.
Ask the union rep how **automated rosters** can be appealed.
feel: I'm **anxious** about fewer shifts, though physical work remains for now.
S1.quote: A screen can't take responsibility for a safe work zone.
fieldNote: He sees planning as a likely change but puts **field safety** under human judgment.
His concern centers on junior **roster hours**, not an immediate loss of the trade.

steps.text: Ask the crew lead for more supervised pole assignments
Ask the union rep how to appeal software-made crew rosters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too soon for me to pretend I know what the company will do. I'd tell the crew the wire work is still real, but I'd ask what happens to the planning desk and the number of crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the new system can schedule a repair, but a crew still has to isolate the circuit and prove it is dead. Nobody should climb because a machine guessed the line was safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep working until robots arrive, but five years is not a long runway when I have no savings. If the company cuts crews before then, I could be back looking for hourly work with no easy local alternative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd ask the union to press for paid retraining time and clear notice before cuts. In 2028 I wouldn't move into planning or records as a safe career, since AGI can do that thinking work. In 2029, if I still have shifts, I'd take an employer-paid electrical safety course and keep working while the field jobs remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me anxious, and the short notice makes my stomach turn. I could try another physical trade, but I don't know which one stays out of reach of robots after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mara when you got home after hearing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Mara that I want us to keep the mortgage current and avoid borrowing for a car this year. We share an old hatchback, so I'd rather repair it than add a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want to avoid debt, but you also said retraining might be needed; how would you manage the cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I can't solve with today's pay. I'd ask for training through the employer or union, because paying tuition myself would mean missing a mortgage payment, and I won't call office planning safe after AGI.

say: I say a crew must **test a circuit** before anyone climbs.
I would ask the company for **notice** before it cuts crews.
think: I may have work until the **2031 robots**, but five years is little time without savings.
I don't know a **lasting trade** that robots won't reach later.
do: Ask the union for **paid training time** and clear notice before cuts.
Repair our shared car instead of taking on **new debt**.
Take an employer-paid **electrical safety course** in 2029 while keeping available shifts.
feel: The short warning leaves me **anxious**, with no clear alternative trade.
S2.quote: Nobody should climb because a machine guessed the line was safe.
fieldNote: He distinguishes hands-on work from vulnerable **planning and records** roles.
He wants training but his **mortgage budget** cannot absorb tuition or lost wages.
He sees **robots** as a later threat but cannot finance private retraining now.

steps.text: Ask the union to seek paid retraining time and advance notice
Repair the shared hatchback instead of borrowing for a replacement
Take the employer-paid electrical safety course in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives the company time to explain its plan, and gives me time to ask questions while I still have a crew. The hands-on part lasts longer than office work, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the warning to talk about safe staffing before the planning system arrives. The company shouldn't let a screen set crew size without asking what the job needs on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have five years before thinking AI and about eight before robots, if the dates hold. That is time to build experience, but linework is not a permanent refuge, and I might still be junior when changes land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for a written path from helper work into a certified crew role, with paid training days. In the first year after 2031, I would stay with field repairs while they remain, and look at another trade only after seeing an actual vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but less cornered than with two years' warning. There is room to learn the work properly, though our small cushion means I can't wait until the last month to think about income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real sign that you should look for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company stops training crew members or starts cancelling field shifts, I'd ask around at the water utility and road crews. I wouldn't assume those jobs are safe; I'd check their pay and equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to put in that written path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date for each qualification, paid hours to train, and whether the company will keep junior workers on the roster. If they can't say that, five years of warning is only a calendar.

say: I say **five years** is enough time to discuss safe crew staffing.
I tell people field repairs last longer than office work, but are not a **permanent refuge**.
think: I could gain experience before **2031**, but I may still be junior.
A thin cushion and two children mean I need to watch **income signs** before the deadline.
do: Ask for a written path to a **certified crew role** with paid training.
Check actual vacancies if **field shifts** begin to disappear.
feel: I feel **anxious but less cornered** than with two years' warning.
S3.quote: The hands-on part lasts longer than office work, but not forever.
fieldNote: He treats extra time as a chance to gain **qualifications**, not a guarantee.
He would check real pay and equipment before considering adjacent **utility work**.

steps.text: Request paid training toward a certified line crew role
Check water utility or road crew vacancies if field shifts are cancelled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me a chance to become fully trained and see whether the company still needs crews. The warning matters, but I don't know the 2039 job list. Nobody can promise which physical jobs will still be there in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start planning now, not because every lineworker disappears tomorrow, but because ten years passes quickly when you're paying a mortgage each month. The company should tell crews what changes it can actually see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when thinking AGI arrived and about 56 when the robots did. I could build years of experience, but records or control-room planning won't protect me once AGI can do thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd finish my apprenticeship steps and ask about the next certificate, while keeping our monthly costs plain. In 2037, if I still have field shifts, I'd review my hours and wages, take any employer-paid training I can get, and decide what we can afford to help our older child study further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds manageable until I remember our savings are less than a month's expenses today, with two children and a mortgage. I'm anxious about that immediate lack of room, though the longer warning gives me choices to investigate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you make a decision before the decade is up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a real training schedule, wages during training, and honest numbers about how many crews the company expects to keep. A poster saying workers can adapt would not cover the mortgage while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any plans with Mara because of the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be careful about promising to help our older child pay for further study until we knew how my wages were changing. At 23 in 2036, that is a real family decision rather than a school-age cost.

say: I say ten years gives crews time to **plan**, but no one can promise the 2039 job map.
I want the company to share **real staffing plans**, not a slogan.
think: I could gain line experience, but **desk duties** won't protect me after thinking AGI.
Today's savings cover less than a month, so the long warning doesn't ease **current pressure**.
do: Finish my apprenticeship steps and ask about the **next certificate**.
Review my **field hours and wages** in 2037 and take employer-paid training if it is offered.
Set a **study budget** for our older child after checking the mortgage and my wages.
feel: The decade gives options, yet **today's thin savings** still make me anxious about my family.
S4.quote: Nobody can promise which physical jobs will still be there in 2039.
fieldNote: He translates the decade into a **training path** and a family education decision.
He rejects office planning as a fallback after AGI can do **thinking work**.

steps.text: Complete apprenticeship steps and ask about the next lineworker certificate
Take employer-paid training in 2037 if field shifts and courses are available
Set further-study support for the older child after checking wages and mortgage costs

portrait: Aaron is a **43-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner, two children and a mortgage.
He values careful **field work** and distrusts screens until he understands what they record.
His **thin savings** make lost shifts a real concern while he supports two children.
He wants paid training and clear crew plans, while accepting no trade is guaranteed safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because five years until robots is not much time for someone with almost no savings. Paid training time and notice before crew cuts would help more than a promise to be positive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask how a junior worker gets enough supervised hours to qualify when the crew is busy. I want to be useful and careful. A certificate takes time that the mortgage clock doesn't give back.

headlineQuote: A certificate takes time that the mortgage clock doesn't give back.
portrait: I'm a **43-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner, two children and a mortgage.
I value careful **field work** and don't trust a screen before I understand what it records.
My **thin savings** make lost shifts a real concern even when work remains physical.
I want **paid training** and clear crew plans, while accepting no trade is guaranteed safe.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries me most because robots may arrive around 2031 before I build a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training time** and notice before crew cuts would give me a practical path.
